# Multi Search Engine v2.0.1

Integration of 17 search engines for web crawling without API keys.

## Search Engines

### Domestic (8)
- **Baidu**: `https://www.baidu.com/s?wd={keyword}`
- **Bing CN**: `https://cn.bing.com/search?q={keyword}&ensearch=0`
- **Bing INT**: `https://cn.bing.com/search?q={keyword}&ensearch=1`
- **360**: `https://www.so.com/s?q={keyword}`
- **Sogou**: `https://sogou.com/web?query={keyword}`
- **WeChat**: `https://wx.sogou.com/weixin?type=2&query={keyword}`
- **Toutiao**: `https://so.toutiao.com/search?keyword={keyword}`
- **Jisilu**: `https://www.jisilu.cn/explore/?keyword={keyword}`

### International (9)
- **Google**: `https://www.google.com/search?q={keyword}`
- **Google HK**: `https://www.google.com.hk/search?q={keyword}`
- **DuckDuckGo**: `https://duckduckgo.com/html/?q={keyword}`
- **Yahoo**: `https://search.yahoo.com/search?p={keyword}`
- **Startpage**: `https://www.startpage.com/sp/search?query={keyword}`
- **Brave**: `https://search.brave.com/search?q={keyword}`
- **Ecosia**: `https://www.ecosia.org/search?q={keyword}`
- **Qwant**: `https://www.qwant.com/?q={keyword}`
- **WolframAlpha**: `https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i={keyword}`

## Quick Examples

```javascript
// Basic search
web_fetch({"url": "https://www.google.com/search?q=python+tutorial"})

// Site-specific
web_fetch({"url": "https://www.google.com/search?q=site:github.com+react"})

// File type
web_fetch({"url": "https://www.google.com/search?q=machine+learning+filetype:pdf"})

// Time filter (past week)
web_fetch({"url": "https://www.google.com/search?q=ai+news&tbs=qdr:w"})

// Privacy search
web_fetch({"url": "https://duckduckgo.com/html/?q=privacy+tools"})

// DuckDuckGo Bangs
web_fetch({"url": "https://duckduckgo.com/html/?q=!gh+tensorflow"})

// Knowledge calculation
web_fetch({"url": "https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=100+USD+to+CNY"})
```

## Advanced Operators

| Operator | Example | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `site:` | `site:github.com python` | Search within site |
| `filetype:` | `filetype:pdf report` | Specific file type |
| `""` | `"machine learning"` | Exact match |
| `-` | `python -snake` | Exclude term |
| `OR` | `cat OR dog` | Either term |

## Time Filters

| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `tbs=qdr:h` | Past hour |
| `tbs=qdr:d` | Past day |
| `tbs=qdr:w` | Past week |
| `tbs=qdr:m` | Past month |
| `tbs=qdr:y` | Past year |

## Privacy Engines

- **DuckDuckGo**: No tracking
- **Startpage**: Google results + privacy
- **Brave**: Independent index
- **Qwant**: EU GDPR compliant

## Bangs Shortcuts (DuckDuckGo)

| Bang | Destination |
|------|-------------|
| `!g` | Google |
| `!gh` | GitHub |
| `!so` | Stack Overflow |
| `!w` | Wikipedia |
| `!yt` | YouTube |

## WolframAlpha Queries

- Math: `integrate x^2 dx`
- Conversion: `100 USD to CNY`
- Stocks: `AAPL stock`
- Weather: `weather in Beijing`

## Documentation

- `references/advanced-search.md` - Domestic search guide
- `references/international-search.md` - International search guide
- `CHANGELOG.md` - Version history

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The exploration of [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(planet)) has long had a minor role in the space interests of the world. It is the least explored [inner planet](/wiki/Terrestrial_planet).[[1]](#cite_note-JHUAPL-1) As of 2025, the [Mariner 10](/wiki/Mariner_10), [MESSENGER](/wiki/MESSENGER), and [BepiColombo](/wiki/BepiColombo) missions have been the only spacecraft that have made close observations of [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(planet)). MESSENGER made three [flybys](/wiki/Planetary_flyby) before entering orbit around Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-Munsell2006b-2) BepiColombo, a joint mission between the [Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency](/wiki/Japan_Aerospace_Exploration_Agency) (JAXA) and the [European Space Agency](/wiki/European_Space_Agency), is to deliver two [probes](/wiki/Space_probe) into Mercury orbit in 2026, having previously made six flybys of the tiny planet. MESSENGER and BepiColombo are intended to gather complementary data to help scientists understand many of the mysteries discovered by Mariner 10's flybys.

Compared to other planets, Mercury is difficult to explore. The speed required to reach it is relatively high, and its proximity to the [Sun](/wiki/Sun) makes it difficult to maneuver a spacecraft into a stable orbit around it.[[3]](#cite_note-ESA2007-3) As a result, all spacecraft sent to visit Mercury as of 2025 have required a complex trajectory of gravity assists, highly efficient [ion propulsion](/wiki/Ion_propulsion), or both. The thermal environment around Mercury is also challenging, with probes utilizing sunshields, specially designed materials, or radiators to survive the heat so close to the Sun.

## Interest in Mercury
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Exploration_of_Mercury&action=edit&section=1)]

Few missions have targeted Mercury because it is very difficult to obtain a [satellite orbit](/wiki/Orbital_spaceflight) around the planet. Mercury [orbits](/wiki/Orbit) the Sun very quickly (between 24.25 miles per second (39.03 km/s) and 30 miles per second (48 km/s)), so spacecraft must be travelling very fast to reach it. Mercury's close proximity to the Sun means that spacecraft are accelerated even further by the Sun's [gravitational](/wiki/Gravitation) pull, requiring significant fuel expenditure in order to decelerate for [orbit insertion](/wiki/Orbit_insertion).[[4]](#cite_note-ley196807-4) Mercury's lack of any significant [atmosphere](/wiki/Atmosphere)[[5]](#cite_note-Munsell2006a-5) poses further challenges because it precludes [aerobraking](/wiki/Aerobraking). Thus a landing mission would have even more demanding fuel requirements.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

[Mariner 10](/wiki/Mariner_10) was a [NASA](/wiki/NASA) [probe](/wiki/Space_probe) whose primary objective was to observe the atmosphere, surface, and physical characteristics of Mercury and [Venus](/wiki/Venus). It was a low-cost mission completed for under [$](/wiki/United_States_dollar)98 million.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Mariner 10 was launched at 12:45 am [EST](/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone) on November 3, 1973, from [Cape Canaveral](/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center).[[8]](#cite_note-Dunne1978p45-8) Since Mercury is so close to the Sun it was too difficult to incorporate an orbit around Mercury in the route so Mariner 10 orbited the Sun. In order to reach its destination, the satellite was [accelerated](/wiki/Gravity_assist) with the [gravity field](/wiki/Gravitational_field) of Venus. It then passed close to Mercury on March 29, 1974, as it flew towards the Sun. This was the first observation made of Mercury at close range. After the encounter Mariner 10 was in an orbit around the Sun such that for every one of its orbits Mercury made two, and the spacecraft and the planet would be able to meet again. This allowed the probe to pass by Mercury two additional times before completing the mission; these encounters were made on September 21, 1974, and March 16, 1975. However, since the same side of Mercury was illuminated during each of the flybys, at the conclusion of the mission Mariner 10 had only photographed approximately 45 percent of its surface.[[9]](#cite_note-9) The mission ended when the probe's [attitude control](/wiki/Spacecraft_attitude_control) gas ran out on March 24, 1975. As the spacecraft was no longer controllable without its nitrogen gas thrusters, a command was sent to the probe to shut down its transmitter.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

The close observations collected two important sets of data. The probe detected Mercury's [magnetic field](/wiki/Magnetic_field), which is very similar to Earth's. This was a surprise to scientists, because Mercury spins so slowly on its axis. Secondly, visual data was provided, which showed the high number of [craters](/wiki/Impact_crater) on the surface of the planet.[[11]](#cite_note-11) The visual data also allowed scientists to determine that Mercury had "not experienced significant [crustal modification](/wiki/Geology_of_Mercury)”.[[12]](#cite_note-12) This also added to the mystery of the Mercurian magnetic field, as it was previously believed that the planet's magnetic fields are caused by a dynamo effect of a molten core, but the lack of crustal change brought this idea into question. The visual data also allowed scientists to investigate the composition and age of the planet.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

/wiki/File:Animation_of_MESSENGER_trajectory_around_Mercury.gifAnimation of [MESSENGER](/wiki/MESSENGER)'s trajectory around [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(planet)) from March 15, 2011 to December 30, 2014
   [MESSENGER](/wiki/MESSENGER) ·   [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(planet))
/wiki/File:MESSENGER_first_photo_of_unseen_side_of_mercury.jpgPhotograph of Mercury from MESSENGER's first flyby of the planet, showing many previously unknown features
[MESSENGER](/wiki/MESSENGER) (Mercury Surface, Space Environment, Geochemistry, and Ranging) was a [NASA](/wiki/NASA) orbital probe of Mercury. It was launched from [Cape Canaveral](/wiki/Cape_Canaveral_Air_Force_Station) on August 3, 2004, after a one-day delay due to bad weather.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) It took the probe about six and a half years before it entered orbit around Mercury. In order to correct the speed of the satellite it undertook several gravitational slingshot flybys of Earth, Venus and Mercury. It passed by the Earth in February 2005 and then Venus in October 2006[[2]](#cite_note-Munsell2006b-2) and in October 2007. Furthermore, the probe made three passes of Mercury, one in January 2008, one in October 2008 and one in September 2009, before entering orbit in 2011. During these flybys of Mercury, enough data was collected to produce images of over 95% of its surface.

MESSENGER used a chemical [bi-propellant](/wiki/Bipropellant_rocket) system both to reach Mercury and achieve orbit.[[16]](#cite_note-McNutt2004-16) MESSENGER's scheduled orbital insertion took place successfully on March 18, 2011. In November 2012, NASA reported that MESSENGER had discovered a possibility of both [water ice](/wiki/Ice) and organic compounds in permanently shadowed craters in Mercury's north pole.[[17]](#cite_note-17) The mission was scheduled to end sometime in 2012, when it was estimated that there would no longer be enough fuel to maintain the probe's orbit.[[18]](#cite_note-18) The primary mission was completed on March 17, 2012, having collected close to 100,000 images.[[19]](#cite_note-jhuap14-19) MESSENGER achieved 100% mapping of Mercury on March 6, 2013, and completed its first year-long extended mission on March 17, 2013.[[20]](#cite_note-ExMissionCompleted2013-20) In February 2013, NASA published the most detailed and accurate 3D map of Mercury to date, assembled from thousands of images taken by MESSENGER.[[21]](#cite_note-21) The probe continued collecting scientific data until April 30, 2015, when under a decaying orbit, the probe was allowed to crash onto the surface of Mercury.[[22]](#cite_note-Extension_2015-22)

/wiki/File:Baranauskas_crater_MESSENGER_WAC_IGF_to_RGB.jpgBaranauskas crater (center) on Mercury. Bright patches within the crater are [Hollows](/wiki/Hollows_(Mercury)). Approximate color representation combining three images acquired by MESSENGER
The MESSENGER mission was designed to study the characteristics and environment of Mercury from orbit. Specifically, the scientific objectives of the mission were:[[23]](#cite_note-Objectives1-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24)

- characterize the chemical composition of Mercury's surface.

- study the geologic history.

- elucidate the nature of [Mercury's magnetic field](/wiki/Mercury%27s_magnetic_field) ([magnetosphere](/wiki/Magnetosphere)).

- determine the size and state of the [core](/wiki/Planetary_core).

- determine the volatile inventory at the poles.

- study the nature of Mercury's [exosphere](/wiki/Exosphere).

/wiki/File:BepiColombo_spacecraft_model.pngArtist's depiction of the BepiColombo mission, with the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (left) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (right)

BepiColombo consists of two spacecraft: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mio (Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, MMO). Each orbiter has a distinct purpose: the MPO is to acquire images in several wavelengths to map the surface and exosphere composition of Mercury, and Mio's is to study the [magnetosphere](/wiki/Magnetosphere). It is a joint mission of the European Space Agency and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency; ESA provided the MPO, while JAXA provided Mio.[[3]](#cite_note-ESA2007-3) The BepiColombo mission will attempt to gather enough information to answer these questions:

- What can we learn from Mercury about the composition of the [solar nebula](/wiki/Solar_nebula) and the formation of the [planetary system](/wiki/Planetary_system)?

- Why is Mercury's normalized density markedly higher than that of all other terrestrial planets, as well as the [Moon](/wiki/Moon)?

- Is the core of Mercury liquid or solid?

- Is Mercury tectonically active today?

- Why does such a small planet possess an intrinsic magnetic field, while Venus, Mars, and the Moon do not have any?

- Why do [spectroscopic](/wiki/Spectroscopic) observations not reveal the presence of any [iron](/wiki/Iron), while this [element](/wiki/Chemical_element) is supposedly the major constituent of Mercury?

- Do the permanently shadowed craters of the polar regions contain [sulfur](/wiki/Sulfur) or water ice?

- What are the production mechanisms of the [exosphere](/wiki/Exosphere)?

- In the absence of any [ionosphere](/wiki/Ionosphere), how does the magnetic field interact with the [solar wind](/wiki/Solar_wind)?

- Is Mercury's magnetised environment characterized by features reminiscent of the [aurorae](/wiki/Aurora_(astronomy)), [radiation belts](/wiki/Van_Allen_radiation_belt) and [magnetospheric](/wiki/Magnetosphere) substorms observed on Earth?

- Since the advance of Mercury's [perihelion](/wiki/Apsis) was explained in terms of [space-time](/wiki/Space-time) curvature, can we take advantage of the proximity of the Sun to test [general relativity](/wiki/General_relativity) with improved accuracy?[[3]](#cite_note-ESA2007-3)

Like Mariner 10 and MESSENGER, BepiColombo used [gravity slingshots](/wiki/Gravity_assist) from Venus and Earth. BepiColombo uses [solar electric propulsion](/wiki/Solar_electric_propulsion) (ion engines) and similar maneuvers at the Moon, Venus, and Mercury. These techniques slowed the orbiters as they approach Mercury. It is essential to avoid using fuel to slow the orbiters as they get closer to the Sun to minimize the gravitational influence of the Sun.[[2]](#cite_note-Munsell2006b-2)

The BepiColombo mission was approved in November 2009,[[25]](#cite_note-25) and successfully launched on October 20, 2018. It was scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury in December 2025, but a loss of performance of its ion thrusters have delayed this to November 2026.[[26]](#cite_note-26) Its primary mission will last until April 2028, with a possible extension to April 2029.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

[Mercury-P](/wiki/Mercury-P) (Меркурий-П/Mercury-Landing) is a proposed lander mission to Mercury by the Russian Space Agency. The probe would utilize solar-electric propulsion to reach Mercury orbit, before deploying a semi-hard lander based on those developed for the [Mars-96](/wiki/Mars-96) project.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

In August 2020, the [Applied Physics Laboratory](/wiki/Applied_Physics_Laboratory) proposed the Mercury Lander for NASA's [New Frontiers program](/wiki/New_Frontiers_program). If selected, it would launch in March 2035 and land in April 2045.[[29]](#cite_note-Space@APL-29)

[Mercury Observer](/wiki/Mercury_Observer) was a cancelled proposal in the [Planetary Observer](/wiki/Planetary_Observer) program, which was terminated after the loss of its first mission, [Mars Observer](/wiki/Mars_Observer).

## Comparison of MESSENGER and BepiColombo
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Exploration_of_Mercury&action=edit&section=10)]

BepiColombo was designed to complement the findings of MESSENGER and is equipped with far more measuring equipment than MESSENGER to obtain a larger range of data. The orbital patterns of BepiColombo and MESSENGER are significantly different.[[16]](#cite_note-McNutt2004-16)

The BepiColombo mission comprises two satellites launched together: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mio (Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, MMO). The MPO will have a circular orbit much closer to Mercury. The reason for this orbit is that the MPO will be measuring the composition of the surface and exosphere, and the close orbit will aid on data quality. On the other hand, Mio (MMO) and MESSENGER took largely [elliptical orbits](/wiki/Elliptical_orbit). This is because of the stability of this orbit and the lower amount of fuel required to obtain and maintain this orbit.[[30]](#cite_note-Mukai2006-30) Another reason for the different orbits of Mio and MESSENGER was so that the data collected by Mio would complement that of MESSENGER, providing more accurate measurements.[[16]](#cite_note-McNutt2004-16)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The exploration of [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(planet)) has long had a minor role in the space interests of the world. It is the least explored [inner planet](/wiki/Terrestrial_planet).[[1]](#cite_note-JHUAPL-1) As of 2025, the [Mariner 10](/wiki/Mariner_10), [MESSENGER](/wiki/MESSENGER), and [BepiColombo](/wiki/BepiColombo) missions have been the only spacecraft that have made close observations of [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(planet)). MESSENGER made three [flybys](/wiki/Planetary_flyby) before entering orbit around Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-Munsell2006b-2) BepiColombo, a joint mission between the [Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency](/wiki/Japan_Aerospace_Exploration_Agency) (JAXA) and the [European Space Agency](/wiki/European_Space_Agency), is to deliver two [probes](/wiki/Space_probe) into Mercury orbit in 2026, having previously made six flybys of the tiny planet. MESSENGER and BepiColombo are intended to gather complementary data to help scientists understand many of the mysteries discovered by Mariner 10's flybys.

Compared to other planets, Mercury is difficult to explore. The speed required to reach it is relatively high, and its proximity to the [Sun](/wiki/Sun) makes it difficult to maneuver a spacecraft into a stable orbit around it.[[3]](#cite_note-ESA2007-3) As a result, all spacecraft sent to visit Mercury as of 2025 have required a complex trajectory of gravity assists, highly efficient [ion propulsion](/wiki/Ion_propulsion), or both. The thermal environment around Mercury is also challenging, with probes utilizing sunshields, specially designed materials, or radiators to survive the heat so close to the Sun.

## Interest in Mercury
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Exploration_of_Mercury&action=edit&section=1)]

Few missions have targeted Mercury because it is very difficult to obtain a [satellite orbit](/wiki/Orbital_spaceflight) around the planet. Mercury [orbits](/wiki/Orbit) the Sun very quickly (between 24.25 miles per second (39.03 km/s) and 30 miles per second (48 km/s)), so spacecraft must be travelling very fast to reach it. Mercury's close proximity to the Sun means that spacecraft are accelerated even further by the Sun's [gravitational](/wiki/Gravitation) pull, requiring significant fuel expenditure in order to decelerate for [orbit insertion](/wiki/Orbit_insertion).[[4]](#cite_note-ley196807-4) Mercury's lack of any significant [atmosphere](/wiki/Atmosphere)[[5]](#cite_note-Munsell2006a-5) poses further challenges because it precludes [aerobraking](/wiki/Aerobraking). Thus a landing mission would have even more demanding fuel requirements.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

[Mariner 10](/wiki/Mariner_10) was a [NASA](/wiki/NASA) [probe](/wiki/Space_probe) whose primary objective was to observe the atmosphere, surface, and physical characteristics of Mercury and [Venus](/wiki/Venus). It was a low-cost mission completed for under [$](/wiki/United_States_dollar)98 million.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Mariner 10 was launched at 12:45 am [EST](/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone) on November 3, 1973, from [Cape Canaveral](/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center).[[8]](#cite_note-Dunne1978p45-8) Since Mercury is so close to the Sun it was too difficult to incorporate an orbit around Mercury in the route so Mariner 10 orbited the Sun. In order to reach its destination, the satellite was [accelerated](/wiki/Gravity_assist) with the [gravity field](/wiki/Gravitational_field) of Venus. It then passed close to Mercury on March 29, 1974, as it flew towards the Sun. This was the first observation made of Mercury at close range. After the encounter Mariner 10 was in an orbit around the Sun such that for every one of its orbits Mercury made two, and the spacecraft and the planet would be able to meet again. This allowed the probe to pass by Mercury two additional times before completing the mission; these encounters were made on September 21, 1974, and March 16, 1975. However, since the same side of Mercury was illuminated during each of the flybys, at the conclusion of the mission Mariner 10 had only photographed approximately 45 percent of its surface.[[9]](#cite_note-9) The mission ended when the probe's [attitude control](/wiki/Spacecraft_attitude_control) gas ran out on March 24, 1975. As the spacecraft was no longer controllable without its nitrogen gas thrusters, a command was sent to the probe to shut down its transmitter.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

The close observations collected two important sets of data. The probe detected Mercury's [magnetic field](/wiki/Magnetic_field), which is very similar to Earth's. This was a surprise to scientists, because Mercury spins so slowly on its axis. Secondly, visual data was provided, which showed the high number of [craters](/wiki/Impact_crater) on the surface of the planet.[[11]](#cite_note-11) The visual data also allowed scientists to determine that Mercury had "not experienced significant [crustal modification](/wiki/Geology_of_Mercury)”.[[12]](#cite_note-12) This also added to the mystery of the Mercurian magnetic field, as it was previously believed that the planet's magnetic fields are caused by a dynamo effect of a molten core, but the lack of crustal change brought this idea into question. The visual data also allowed scientists to investigate the composition and age of the planet.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

/wiki/File:Animation_of_MESSENGER_trajectory_around_Mercury.gifAnimation of [MESSENGER](/wiki/MESSENGER)'s trajectory around [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(planet)) from March 15, 2011 to December 30, 2014
   [MESSENGER](/wiki/MESSENGER) ·   [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(planet))
/wiki/File:MESSENGER_first_photo_of_unseen_side_of_mercury.jpgPhotograph of Mercury from MESSENGER's first flyby of the planet, showing many previously unknown features
[MESSENGER](/wiki/MESSENGER) (Mercury Surface, Space Environment, Geochemistry, and Ranging) was a [NASA](/wiki/NASA) orbital probe of Mercury. It was launched from [Cape Canaveral](/wiki/Cape_Canaveral_Air_Force_Station) on August 3, 2004, after a one-day delay due to bad weather.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) It took the probe about six and a half years before it entered orbit around Mercury. In order to correct the speed of the satellite it undertook several gravitational slingshot flybys of Earth, Venus and Mercury. It passed by the Earth in February 2005 and then Venus in October 2006[[2]](#cite_note-Munsell2006b-2) and in October 2007. Furthermore, the probe made three passes of Mercury, one in January 2008, one in October 2008 and one in September 2009, before entering orbit in 2011. During these flybys of Mercury, enough data was collected to produce images of over 95% of its surface.

MESSENGER used a chemical [bi-propellant](/wiki/Bipropellant_rocket) system both to reach Mercury and achieve orbit.[[16]](#cite_note-McNutt2004-16) MESSENGER's scheduled orbital insertion took place successfully on March 18, 2011. In November 2012, NASA reported that MESSENGER had discovered a possibility of both [water ice](/wiki/Ice) and organic compounds in permanently shadowed craters in Mercury's north pole.[[17]](#cite_note-17) The mission was scheduled to end sometime in 2012, when it was estimated that there would no longer be enough fuel to maintain the probe's orbit.[[18]](#cite_note-18) The primary mission was completed on March 17, 2012, having collected close to 100,000 images.[[19]](#cite_note-jhuap14-19) MESSENGER achieved 100% mapping of Mercury on March 6, 2013, and completed its first year-long extended mission on March 17, 2013.[[20]](#cite_note-ExMissionCompleted2013-20) In February 2013, NASA published the most detailed and accurate 3D map of Mercury to date, assembled from thousands of images taken by MESSENGER.[[21]](#cite_note-21) The probe continued collecting scientific data until April 30, 2015, when under a decaying orbit, the probe was allowed to crash onto the surface of Mercury.[[22]](#cite_note-Extension_2015-22)

/wiki/File:Baranauskas_crater_MESSENGER_WAC_IGF_to_RGB.jpgBaranauskas crater (center) on Mercury. Bright patches within the crater are [Hollows](/wiki/Hollows_(Mercury)). Approximate color representation combining three images acquired by MESSENGER
The MESSENGER mission was designed to study the characteristics and environment of Mercury from orbit. Specifically, the scientific objectives of the mission were:[[23]](#cite_note-Objectives1-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24)

- characterize the chemical composition of Mercury's surface.

- study the geologic history.

- elucidate the nature of [Mercury's magnetic field](/wiki/Mercury%27s_magnetic_field) ([magnetosphere](/wiki/Magnetosphere)).

- determine the size and state of the [core](/wiki/Planetary_core).

- determine the volatile inventory at the poles.

- study the nature of Mercury's [exosphere](/wiki/Exosphere).

/wiki/File:BepiColombo_spacecraft_model.pngArtist's depiction of the BepiColombo mission, with the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (left) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (right)

BepiColombo consists of two spacecraft: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mio (Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, MMO). Each orbiter has a distinct purpose: the MPO is to acquire images in several wavelengths to map the surface and exosphere composition of Mercury, and Mio's is to study the [magnetosphere](/wiki/Magnetosphere). It is a joint mission of the European Space Agency and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency; ESA provided the MPO, while JAXA provided Mio.[[3]](#cite_note-ESA2007-3) The BepiColombo mission will attempt to gather enough information to answer these questions:

- What can we learn from Mercury about the composition of the [solar nebula](/wiki/Solar_nebula) and the formation of the [planetary system](/wiki/Planetary_system)?

- Why is Mercury's normalized density markedly higher than that of all other terrestrial planets, as well as the [Moon](/wiki/Moon)?

- Is the core of Mercury liquid or solid?

- Is Mercury tectonically active today?

- Why does such a small planet possess an intrinsic magnetic field, while Venus, Mars, and the Moon do not have any?

- Why do [spectroscopic](/wiki/Spectroscopic) observations not reveal the presence of any [iron](/wiki/Iron), while this [element](/wiki/Chemical_element) is supposedly the major constituent of Mercury?

- Do the permanently shadowed craters of the polar regions contain [sulfur](/wiki/Sulfur) or water ice?

- What are the production mechanisms of the [exosphere](/wiki/Exosphere)?

- In the absence of any [ionosphere](/wiki/Ionosphere), how does the magnetic field interact with the [solar wind](/wiki/Solar_wind)?

- Is Mercury's magnetised environment characterized by features reminiscent of the [aurorae](/wiki/Aurora_(astronomy)), [radiation belts](/wiki/Van_Allen_radiation_belt) and [magnetospheric](/wiki/Magnetosphere) substorms observed on Earth?

- Since the advance of Mercury's [perihelion](/wiki/Apsis) was explained in terms of [space-time](/wiki/Space-time) curvature, can we take advantage of the proximity of the Sun to test [general relativity](/wiki/General_relativity) with improved accuracy?[[3]](#cite_note-ESA2007-3)

Like Mariner 10 and MESSENGER, BepiColombo used [gravity slingshots](/wiki/Gravity_assist) from Venus and Earth. BepiColombo uses [solar electric propulsion](/wiki/Solar_electric_propulsion) (ion engines) and similar maneuvers at the Moon, Venus, and Mercury. These techniques slowed the orbiters as they approach Mercury. It is essential to avoid using fuel to slow the orbiters as they get closer to the Sun to minimize the gravitational influence of the Sun.[[2]](#cite_note-Munsell2006b-2)

The BepiColombo mission was approved in November 2009,[[25]](#cite_note-25) and successfully launched on October 20, 2018. It was scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury in December 2025, but a loss of performance of its ion thrusters have delayed this to November 2026.[[26]](#cite_note-26) Its primary mission will last until April 2028, with a possible extension to April 2029.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

[Mercury-P](/wiki/Mercury-P) (Меркурий-П/Mercury-Landing) is a proposed lander mission to Mercury by the Russian Space Agency. The probe would utilize solar-electric propulsion to reach Mercury orbit, before deploying a semi-hard lander based on those developed for the [Mars-96](/wiki/Mars-96) project.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

In August 2020, the [Applied Physics Laboratory](/wiki/Applied_Physics_Laboratory) proposed the Mercury Lander for NASA's [New Frontiers program](/wiki/New_Frontiers_program). If selected, it would launch in March 2035 and land in April 2045.[[29]](#cite_note-Space@APL-29)

[Mercury Observer](/wiki/Mercury_Observer) was a cancelled proposal in the [Planetary Observer](/wiki/Planetary_Observer) program, which was terminated after the loss of its first mission, [Mars Observer](/wiki/Mars_Observer).

## Comparison of MESSENGER and BepiColombo
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Exploration_of_Mercury&action=edit&section=10)]

BepiColombo was designed to complement the findings of MESSENGER and is equipped with far more measuring equipment than MESSENGER to obtain a larger range of data. The orbital patterns of BepiColombo and MESSENGER are significantly different.[[16]](#cite_note-McNutt2004-16)

The BepiColombo mission comprises two satellites launched together: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mio (Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, MMO). The MPO will have a circular orbit much closer to Mercury. The reason for this orbit is that the MPO will be measuring the composition of the surface and exosphere, and the close orbit will aid on data quality. On the other hand, Mio (MMO) and MESSENGER took largely [elliptical orbits](/wiki/Elliptical_orbit). This is because of the stability of this orbit and the lower amount of fuel required to obtain and maintain this orbit.[[30]](#cite_note-Mukai2006-30) Another reason for the different orbits of Mio and MESSENGER was so that the data collected by Mio would complement that of MESSENGER, providing more accurate measurements.[[16]](#cite_note-McNutt2004-16)

Project Mercury was the first [human spaceflight](/wiki/Human_spaceflight) program of the United States, running from 1958 through 1963. An early highlight of the [Space Race](/wiki/Space_Race), its goal was to put a man into Earth [orbit](/wiki/Orbital_spaceflight) and return him safely, ideally before the [Soviet Union](/wiki/Soviet_Union). Taken over from the [US Air Force](/wiki/US_Air_Force) by the newly created civilian space agency [NASA](/wiki/NASA), it conducted 20 uncrewed developmental flights (some using animals), and six successful flights by [astronauts](/wiki/Astronauts). The program, which took its name from [Roman mythology](/wiki/Mercury_(mythology)), cost $2.83 billion (adjusted for [inflation](/wiki/Inflation)).[[1]](#cite_note-lafleur20100308-1)[[n 1]](#cite_note-5) The astronauts were collectively known as the "[Mercury Seven](/wiki/Mercury_Seven)", and each spacecraft was given a name ending with a "7" by its pilot.

The Space Race began with the 1957 launch of the Soviet [satellite](/wiki/Satellite) [Sputnik 1](/wiki/Sputnik_1). This came as a shock to the American public, and led to the creation of NASA to expedite existing US space exploration efforts, and place most of them under civilian control. After the successful launch of the [Explorer 1](/wiki/Explorer_1) satellite in 1958, crewed spaceflight became the next goal. The Soviet Union put the first human, [cosmonaut](/wiki/Cosmonaut) [Yuri Gagarin](/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin), into a single orbit aboard [Vostok 1](/wiki/Vostok_1) on April 12, 1961. Shortly after this, on May 5, the US launched its first astronaut, [Alan Shepard](/wiki/Alan_Shepard), on a [suborbital](/wiki/Suborbital) flight. Soviet [Gherman Titov](/wiki/Gherman_Titov) followed with a day-long orbital flight in August 1961. The US reached its orbital goal on February 20, 1962, when [John Glenn](/wiki/John_Glenn) made three orbits around the Earth. When Mercury ended in May 1963, both nations had sent six people into space, but the Soviets led the US in total time spent in space.

The Mercury [space capsule](/wiki/Space_capsule) was produced by [McDonnell Aircraft](/wiki/McDonnell_Aircraft), and carried supplies of water, food and oxygen for about one day in a [pressurized cabin](/wiki/Cabin_pressurization). Mercury flights were launched from [Cape Canaveral Air Force Station](/wiki/Cape_Canaveral_Air_Force_Station) in Florida, on [launch vehicles](/wiki/Launch_vehicle) modified from the [Redstone](/wiki/Redstone_MRLV) and [Atlas D](/wiki/Atlas_LV-3B) missiles. The capsule was fitted with a [launch escape rocket](/wiki/Launch_escape_system) to carry it safely away from the launch vehicle in case of a failure. The flight was designed to be controlled from the ground via the [Manned Space Flight Network](/wiki/Manned_Space_Flight_Network), a system of tracking and communications stations; back-up controls were outfitted on board. Small [retrorockets](/wiki/Retrorocket) were used to bring the spacecraft out of its orbit, after which an [ablative heat shield](/wiki/Ablative_heat_shield) protected it from the heat of [atmospheric reentry](/wiki/Atmospheric_entry). Finally, a [parachute](/wiki/Parachute) slowed the craft for a [water landing](/wiki/Splashdown). Both astronaut and capsule were recovered by helicopters deployed from a US Navy ship.

The Mercury project gained popularity, and its missions were followed by millions on radio and TV around the world. Its success laid the groundwork for [Project Gemini](/wiki/Project_Gemini), which carried two astronauts in each capsule and perfected space docking maneuvers essential for crewed [lunar landings](/wiki/Moon_landing) in the subsequent [Apollo program](/wiki/Apollo_program) announced a few weeks after the first crewed Mercury flight.

Project Mercury was officially approved on October 7, 1958, and publicly announced on December 17.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrimwood196312-6)[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966132-7) Originally called Project Astronaut, President [Dwight Eisenhower](/wiki/Dwight_Eisenhower) felt that gave too much attention to the pilot.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200192-8) Instead, the name [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(mythology)) was chosen from [classical mythology](/wiki/Classical_mythology), which had already lent names to rockets like the Greek [Atlas](/wiki/Atlas_(mythology)) and Roman [Jupiter](/wiki/Jupiter_(mythology)) for the [SM-65](/wiki/SM-65_Atlas) and [PGM-19](/wiki/PGM-19_Jupiter) [missiles](/wiki/Missiles).[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966132-7) It absorbed military projects with the same aim, such as the Air Force [Man in Space Soonest](/wiki/Man_in_Space_Soonest).[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966102-9)[[n 2]](#cite_note-11)

Following the end of [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II), a [nuclear arms race](/wiki/Nuclear_arms_race) evolved between the US and the [Soviet Union](/wiki/Soviet_Union) (USSR). Since the USSR did not have bases in the western hemisphere from which to deploy [bomber planes](/wiki/Bomber), [Joseph Stalin](/wiki/Joseph_Stalin) decided to develop [intercontinental ballistic missiles](/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile), which drove a missile race.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200112–14-12) The rocket technology in turn enabled both sides to develop Earth-orbiting satellites for communications, and gathering weather data and [intelligence](/wiki/Geospatial_intelligence).[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200181-13)

Americans were shocked when the Soviet Union placed the first satellite into orbit in October 1957, leading to a growing fear that the US was falling into a "[missile gap](/wiki/Missile_gap)".[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196628,_52-14)[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200181-13) A month later, the Soviets launched [Sputnik 2](/wiki/Sputnik_2), carrying [a dog](/wiki/Laika) into orbit. Though the animal was not recovered alive, it was obvious their goal was human spaceflight.[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200155-15) Unable to disclose details of military space projects, President Eisenhower ordered the creation of a civilian space agency in charge of civilian and scientific space exploration. Based on the federal research agency [National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics](/wiki/National_Advisory_Committee_for_Aeronautics) (NACA), it was named the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA).[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966113-16) The agency achieved its first goal of launching a satellite into space, the [Pioneer 1](/wiki/Pioneer_1), in 1958. The next goal was to put a man there.[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200157,_82-17)

The limit of space (also known as the [Kármán line](/wiki/K%C3%A1rm%C3%A1n_line)) was defined at the time as a minimum altitude of 62 mi (100 km), and the only way to reach it was by using rocket-powered boosters.[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200170-18)[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196613-19) This created risks for the pilot, including explosion, high [g-forces](/wiki/G-force) and vibrations during lift off through a dense atmosphere,[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196644-20) and temperatures of more than 10,000 °F (5,500 °C) from air compression during reentry.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196659-21)

In space, pilots would require pressurized chambers or [space suits](/wiki/Space_suit) to supply fresh air.[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001466-22) While there, they would experience [weightlessness](/wiki/Weightlessness), which could potentially cause disorientation.[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966357-23) Further potential risks included [radiation](/wiki/Space_radiation) and [micrometeoroid](/wiki/Micrometeoroid) strikes, both of which would normally be absorbed in the atmosphere.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196635,_39–40-24) All seemed possible to overcome: experience from satellites suggested micrometeoroid risk was negligible,[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196649-25) and experiments in the early 1950s with simulated weightlessness, high g-forces on humans, and sending animals to the limit of space, all suggested potential problems could be overcome by known technologies.[[24]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196637–38-26) Finally, reentry was studied using the nuclear warheads of ballistic missiles,[[25]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196661-27) which demonstrated a blunt, forward-facing heat shield could solve the problem of heating.[[25]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196661-27)

[T. Keith Glennan](/wiki/T._Keith_Glennan) had been appointed the first Administrator of NASA, with [Hugh L. Dryden](/wiki/Hugh_L._Dryden) (last Director of NACA) as his Deputy, at the creation of the agency on October 1, 1958.[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196698–99-28) Glennan would report to the president through the [National Aeronautics and Space Council](/wiki/National_Space_Council).[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200182-29) The group responsible for Project Mercury was NASA's [Space Task Group](/wiki/Space_Task_Group), and the goals of the program were to orbit a crewed spacecraft around Earth, investigate the pilot's ability to function in space, and to recover both pilot and spacecraft safely.[[28]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966xiii,_134-30) Existing technology and off-the-shelf equipment would be used wherever practical, the simplest and most reliable approach to system design would be followed, and an existing launch vehicle would be employed, together with a progressive test program.[[29]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966134-31) Spacecraft requirements included: a [launch escape system](/wiki/Launch_escape_system) to separate the spacecraft and its occupant from the [launch vehicle](/wiki/Launch_vehicle) in case of impending failure; [attitude control](/wiki/Spacecraft_attitude_control) for orientation of the spacecraft in orbit; a [retrorocket](/wiki/Retrorocket) system to bring the spacecraft out of orbit; drag braking [blunt body](/wiki/Blunt_Body_theory) for [atmospheric reentry](/wiki/Atmospheric_entry); and landing on water.[[29]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966134-31) To communicate with the spacecraft during an orbital mission, an extensive communications network had to be built.[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966143-32) In keeping with his desire to keep from giving the US space program an overtly military flavor, President Eisenhower at first hesitated to give the project top national priority (DX rating under the [Defense Production Act](/wiki/Defense_Production_Act)), which meant that Mercury had to wait in line behind military projects for materials; however, this rating was granted in May 1959, a little more than a year and a half after Sputnik was launched.[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001157-33)

### Contractors and facilities
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Project_Mercury&action=edit&section=4)]

Twelve companies bid to build the Mercury spacecraft on a $20 million ($221 million adjusted for inflation) contract.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966121,_191-34) In January 1959, [McDonnell Aircraft Corporation](/wiki/McDonnell_Aircraft) was chosen to be prime contractor for the spacecraft.[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966137-35) Two weeks earlier, [North American Aviation](/wiki/North_American_Aviation), based in Los Angeles, was awarded a contract for [Little Joe](/wiki/Little_Joe_(rocket)), a small rocket to be used for development of the launch escape system.[[34]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966124-36)[[n 3]](#cite_note-37) The World Wide Tracking Network for communication between the ground and spacecraft during a flight was awarded to the [Western Electric Company](/wiki/Western_Electric).[[35]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966216-38) Redstone rockets for suborbital launches were manufactured in [Huntsville](/wiki/Huntsville,_Alabama), Alabama, by the [Chrysler Corporation](/wiki/Chrysler_Corporation)[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196621-39) and Atlas rockets by [Convair](/wiki/Convair) in San Diego, California.[[37]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001158-40) For crewed launches, the [Atlantic Missile Range](/wiki/Atlantic_Missile_Range) at [Cape Canaveral Air Force Station](/wiki/Cape_Canaveral_Air_Force_Station) in Florida was made available by the USAF.[[38]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200189–90-41) This was also the site of the Mercury Control Center while the computing center of the communication network was in [Goddard Space Center](/wiki/Goddard_Space_Center), Maryland.[[39]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200186-42) Little Joe rockets were launched from [Wallops Island](/wiki/Wallops_Island), Virginia.[[40]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966141-43) Astronaut training took place at [Langley Research Center](/wiki/Langley_Research_Center) in Virginia, [Lewis Flight Propulsion Laboratory](/wiki/Lewis_Flight_Propulsion_Laboratory) in Cleveland, Ohio, and [Naval Air Development Center Johnsville](/wiki/Naval_Air_Development_Center) in Warminster, PA.[[41]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001103–110-44) Langley wind tunnels[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196688-45) together with a rocket sled track at [Holloman Air Force Base](/wiki/Holloman_Air_Force_Base) at Alamogordo, New Mexico were used for aerodynamic studies.[[43]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001248-46) Both Navy and Air Force aircraft were made available for the development of the spacecraft's landing system,[[44]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001172–173-47) and Navy ships and Navy and Marine Corps helicopters were made available for recovery.[[n 4]](#cite_note-49) South of Cape Canaveral the town of [Cocoa Beach](/wiki/Cocoa_Beach) boomed.[[46]](#cite_note-CocoaBeach-50) From here, 75,000 people watched the first American orbital flight being launched in 1962.[[46]](#cite_note-CocoaBeach-50)

- /wiki/File:Wallops_Island_-_GPN-2000-001888.jpg
 [Wallops Island](/wiki/Wallops_Island) test facility, 1961

- /wiki/File:Mercury_control_center_4june1963.jpg
 [Mercury Control Center](/wiki/Mercury_Control_Center), Cape Canaveral, 1963

- /wiki/File:Project-Mercury-facility-map.png
 Location of production and operational facilities of Project Mercury

The Mercury spacecraft's principal designer was [Maxime Faget](/wiki/Maxime_Faget), who started research for human spaceflight during the time of the NACA.[[47]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001150-51) It was 10.8 feet (3.3 m) long and 6.0 feet (1.8 m) wide; with the launch escape system added, the overall length was 25.9 feet (7.9 m).[[48]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001131-52) With 100 cubic feet (2.8 m3) of habitable volume, the capsule was just large enough for a single crew member.[[49]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196647-53) Inside were 120 controls: 55 electrical switches, 30 [fuses](/wiki/Fuse_(electrical)) and 35 mechanical levers.[[50]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966245-54) The heaviest spacecraft, Mercury-Atlas 9, weighed 3,000 pounds (1,400 kg) fully loaded.[[51]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966490-55) Its outer skin was made of [René 41](/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_41), a nickel alloy able to withstand high temperatures.[[52]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001136-56)

The spacecraft was cone shaped, with a neck at the narrow end.[[48]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001131-52) It had a convex base, which carried a heat shield (Item 2 in the diagram below)[[53]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001134–136-57) consisting of an aluminum [honeycomb](/wiki/Honeycomb_structure) covered with multiple layers of [fiberglass](/wiki/Fiberglass).[[54]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966140,_143-58) Strapped to it was a retropack (1)[[55]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001132–134-59) consisting of three rockets deployed to brake the spacecraft during reentry.[[56]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001132-60) Between these were three posigrade rockets: minor rockets for separating the spacecraft from the launch vehicle at orbital insertion.[[57]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966188-61) The straps that held the package could be severed when it was no longer needed.[[58]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001134-62) Next to the heat shield was the pressurized crew compartment (3).[[59]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001136–144-63) Inside, an astronaut would be strapped to a form-fitting seat with instruments in front of him and with his back to the heat shield.[[60]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001136–137-64) Underneath the seat was the environmental control system supplying oxygen and heat,[[61]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001138-65) scrubbing the air of CO2, vapor and odors, and (on orbital flights) collecting urine.[[62]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001139-66) The recovery compartment (4)[[63]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001144–145-67) at the narrow end of the spacecraft contained three parachutes: a drogue to stabilize free fall and two main chutes, a primary and reserve.[[64]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001144-68) Between the heat shield and inner wall of the crew compartment was a landing skirt, deployed by letting down the heat shield before landing.[[65]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001135-69) On top of the recovery compartment was the [antenna](/wiki/Antenna_(radio)) section (5)[[66]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001145–148-70) containing both antennas for communication and scanners for guiding spacecraft orientation.[[67]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001147-71) Attached was a flap used to ensure the spacecraft was faced heat shield first during reentry.[[68]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966199-72) A launch escape system (6) was mounted to the narrow end of the spacecraft[[69]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001179–181-73) containing three small solid-fueled rockets which could be fired briefly in a launch failure to separate the capsule safely from its booster. It would deploy the capsule's parachute for a landing nearby at sea.[[70]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001179-74) (See also [Mission profile](#Mission_profile) for details.)

The Mercury spacecraft did not have an on-board computer, instead relying on all computation for reentry to be calculated by computers on the ground, with their results (retrofire times and firing attitude) then transmitted to the spacecraft by radio while in flight.[[71]](#cite_note-NASAComp1-75)[[72]](#cite_note-DanCompSpace-76) All computer systems used in the Mercury space program were housed in [NASA](/wiki/NASA) facilities on [Earth](/wiki/Earth).[[71]](#cite_note-NASAComp1-75) (See [ground control](#Ground_control) for details.)

### Pilot accommodations
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Project_Mercury&action=edit&section=6)]

/wiki/File:GPN-2000-001027.jpg[John Glenn](/wiki/John_Glenn) wearing his [Mercury space suit](/wiki/Mercury_space_suit)
The astronaut lay in a sitting position with his back to the heat shield, which was found to be the position that best enabled a human to withstand the high [g-forces](/wiki/G-force) of launch and reentry. A fiberglass seat was custom-molded from each astronaut's space-suited body for maximum support. Near his left hand was a manual abort handle to activate the launch escape system if necessary prior to or during liftoff, in case the automatic trigger failed.[[73]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001142-77)

To supplement the onboard environmental control system, he wore a [pressure suit](/wiki/Pressure_suit) with its own [oxygen](/wiki/Oxygen) supply, which would also cool him.[[74]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001191-78) A cabin atmosphere of pure oxygen at a low pressure of 5.5 psi or 38 kPa (equivalent to the [partial pressure](/wiki/Partial_pressure) of oxygen at sea level or the pressure of atmospheric air at an altitude of 24,800 feet or 7,600 metres) was chosen, rather than the atmosphere at sea level.[[75]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGatland1976264-79) This was easier to control,[[76]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001410-80) avoided the risk of [decompression sickness](/wiki/Decompression_sickness) ("the bends"),[[77]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiblin1998-81)[[n 5]](#cite_note-82) and also saved on spacecraft weight. Fires (which never occurred during the course of Project Mercury) would have to be extinguished by emptying the cabin of oxygen.[[62]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001139-66) In such case, or failure of the cabin pressure for any reason, the astronaut could make an emergency return to Earth, relying on his suit for survival.[[78]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196648–49-83)[[62]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001139-66) The astronauts normally flew with their [visor](/wiki/Visor) up, which meant that the suit was not inflated.[[62]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001139-66) With the visor down and the suit inflated, the astronaut could only reach the side and bottom panels, where vital buttons and handles were placed.[[79]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966246-84)

The astronaut also wore [electrodes](/wiki/Electrode) on his chest to record his [heart rhythm](/wiki/Heart_rhythm), a cuff that could take his blood pressure, and a [rectal thermometer](/wiki/Medical_thermometer) to record his temperature (this was replaced by an oral thermometer on the last flight).[[80]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001191,_194-85) Data from these was sent to the ground during the flight.[[74]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001191-78)[[n 6]](#cite_note-87) The astronaut normally drank water and ate food pellets.[[82]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001343–344-88)[[n 7]](#cite_note-89)

Despite the lessons learnt from the [U2](/wiki/Lockheed_U-2) program, which also utilized a pressure suit, initially no urine collection device was included for the Mercury astronauts. An inquiry on the subject was made in February 1961 by a student, but NASA responded by stating that "the first space man is not expected to have 'to go".[[83]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHollins2013-90) The expected short flight times meant that this was overlooked, although after Alan Shepard had a launch delay of four hours, he was forced to urinate in his suit, short-circuiting some of the electrodes monitoring his vital signs. Gus Grissom wore two rubber pants on the second Mercury flight as a crude workaround. It would take until the third flight in February 1962 before a dedicated urine collection device was installed.[[84]](#cite_note-91)

Once in orbit, the spacecraft could be rotated in [yaw, pitch, and roll](/wiki/Yaw,_pitch,_and_roll): along its longitudinal axis (roll), left to right from the astronaut's point of view (yaw), and up or down (pitch).[[85]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196698-92) Movement was created by [rocket-propelled](/wiki/Rocket_engine) thrusters which used [hydrogen peroxide](/wiki/Hydrogen_peroxide) as a fuel.[[86]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966499-93)[[87]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001143-94) For orientation, the pilot could look through the window in front of him or he could look at a screen connected to a [periscope](/wiki/Periscope) with a camera which could be turned 360°.[[88]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001141-95)

The Mercury astronauts had taken part in the development of their spacecraft, and insisted that manual control, and a window, be elements of its design.[[89]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200198–99-96) As a result, spacecraft movement and other functions could be controlled three ways: remotely from the ground when passing over a ground station, automatically guided by onboard instruments, or manually by the astronaut, who could replace or override the two other methods. Experience validated the astronauts' insistence on manual controls. Without them, [Gordon Cooper](/wiki/Gordon_Cooper)'s manual reentry during the last flight would not have been possible.[[90]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966501-97)

### Development and production
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Project_Mercury&action=edit&section=7)]

/wiki/File:Technicians_working_in_the_McDonnell_White_Room_on_the_Mercury-crop.jpgSpacecraft production in clean room at [McDonnell Aircraft](/wiki/McDonnell_Aircraft), St. Louis, 1960
The Mercury spacecraft design was modified three times by NASA between 1958 and 1959.[[92]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001152-99) After bidding by potential contractors had been completed, NASA selected the design submitted as "C" in November 1958.[[93]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001153-100) After it failed a test flight in July 1959, a final configuration, "D", emerged.[[94]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001159-101) The heat shield shape had been developed earlier in the 1950s through experiments with ballistic missiles, which had shown a blunt profile would create a shock wave that would lead most of the heat around the spacecraft.[[95]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001149-102) To further protect against heat, either a [heat sink](/wiki/Heat_sink), or an ablative material, could be added to the shield.[[96]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196663-103) The heat sink would remove heat by the flow of the air inside the shock wave, whereas the ablative heat shield would remove heat by a controlled evaporation of the ablative material.[[97]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196664-104) After uncrewed tests, the latter was chosen for crewed flights.[[98]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966206-105) Apart from the capsule design, a [rocket plane](/wiki/Rocket_plane) similar to the existing [X-15](/wiki/X-15) was considered.[[99]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196678–80-106) This approach was still too far from being able to make a spaceflight, and was consequently dropped.[[100]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196672-107)[[n 8]](#cite_note-111) The heat shield and the stability of the spacecraft were tested in [wind tunnels](/wiki/Supersonic_wind_tunnel),[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196688-45) and later in flight.[[104]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001229-112) The launch escape system was developed through uncrewed flights.[[105]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001196-113) During a period of problems with development of the landing parachutes, alternative landing systems such as the [Rogallo glider wing](/wiki/Rogallo_wing) were considered, but ultimately scrapped.[[106]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966198-114)

The spacecraft were produced at [McDonnell Aircraft](/wiki/McDonnell_Aircraft), [St. Louis](/wiki/St._Louis,_Missouri), Missouri, in clean rooms and tested in vacuum chambers at the McDonnell plant.[[107]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001132,_159-115) The spacecraft had close to 600 subcontractors, such as [Garrett AiResearch](/wiki/Garrett_AiResearch) which built the spacecraft's environmental control system.[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966137-35)[[61]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001138-65) Final quality control and preparations of the spacecraft were made at Hangar S at Cape Canaveral.[[108]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001184–188-116)[[n 9]](#cite_note-119) NASA ordered 20 production spacecraft, numbered 1 through 20.[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966137-35) Five of the 20, Nos. 10, 12, 15, 17, and 19, were not flown.[[111]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrimwood1963235–238-120) Spacecraft No. 3 and No. 4 were destroyed during uncrewed test flights.[[111]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrimwood1963235–238-120) Spacecraft No. 11 sank and was recovered from the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean after 38 years.[[111]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrimwood1963235–238-120)[[112]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001402–405-121) Some spacecraft were modified after initial production (refurbished after launch abort, modified for longer missions, etc.).[[n 10]](#cite_note-124) A number of Mercury [boilerplate spacecraft](/wiki/Boilerplate_(spaceflight)) (made from non-flight materials or lacking production spacecraft systems) were also made by NASA and McDonnell.[[115]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966126_&_138-125) They were designed and used to test spacecraft recovery systems and the escape tower.[[116]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196696,_105-126) McDonnell also built the spacecraft simulators used by the astronauts during training,[[117]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001107-127) and adopted the motto "First Free Man in Space".[[118]](#cite_note-logo_history-128)

### Launch escape system testing
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Project_Mercury&action=edit&section=9)]

A 55-foot-long (17 m) launch vehicle called [Little Joe](/wiki/Little_Joe_(rocket)) was used for uncrewed tests of the launch escape system, using a Mercury capsule with an escape tower mounted on it.[[119]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001197-129)[[120]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966638-130) Its main purpose was to test the system at [max q](/wiki/Max_q), when aerodynamic forces against the spacecraft peaked, making separation of the launch vehicle and spacecraft most difficult.[[121]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001223-131) It was also the point at which the astronaut was subjected to the heaviest vibrations.[[122]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001284-132) The Little Joe rocket used [solid-fuel](/wiki/Solid-fuel_rocket) propellant and was originally designed in 1958 by NACA for suborbital crewed flights, but was redesigned for Project Mercury to simulate an Atlas-D launch.[[105]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001196-113) It was produced by [North American Aviation](/wiki/North_American_Aviation).[[119]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001197-129) It was not able to change direction; instead its flight depended on the angle from which it was launched.[[123]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001198-133) Its maximum altitude was 100 mi (160 km) fully loaded.[[124]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966125-134) A [Scout launch vehicle](/wiki/Mercury-Scout_1) was used for a single flight intended to evaluate the tracking network; however, it failed and was [destroyed from the ground](/wiki/Range_safety) shortly after launch.[[125]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966392–397-135)

/wiki/File:Chimpanzee_Ham_in_Biopack_Couch_-_cropped.jpg

/wiki/File:Mercury-Atlas_5_Enos_with_handler_(cropped).jpg

The [Mercury-Redstone Launch Vehicle](/wiki/Mercury-Redstone_Launch_Vehicle) was an 83-foot-tall (25 m) (with capsule and escape system) single-stage launch vehicle used for suborbital ([ballistic](/wiki/Ballistic_missile)) flights.[[126]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001206-136) It had a liquid-fueled engine that burned alcohol and liquid oxygen producing about 75,000 pounds-force (330 kN) of thrust, which was not enough for orbital missions.[[126]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001206-136) It was a descendant of the German [V-2](/wiki/V-2_(rocket)),[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196621-39) and developed for the [US Army](/wiki/US_Army) during the early 1950s. It was modified for Project Mercury by removing the warhead and adding a collar for supporting the spacecraft together with material for damping vibrations during launch.[[127]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001207-137) Its rocket motor was produced by [North American Aviation](/wiki/North_American_Aviation) and its direction could be altered during flight by its fins. They worked in two ways: by directing the air around them, or by directing the thrust by their inner parts (or both at the same time).[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196621-39) Both the Atlas-D and Redstone launch vehicles contained an automatic abort sensing system which allowed them to abort a launch by firing the launch escape system if something went wrong.[[128]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001209,_214-138) The [Jupiter](/wiki/Mercury-Jupiter) rocket, also developed by [Wernher von Braun](/wiki/Wernher_von_Braun)'s team at the Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, was considered as well for intermediate Mercury suborbital flights at a higher speed and altitude than Redstone, but this plan was dropped when it turned out that man-rating Jupiter for the Mercury program would actually cost more than flying an Atlas due to economics of scale.[[129]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966151-139)[[130]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrimwood196369-140) Beyond its IRBM function, the Jupiter missile was repurposed only for the short-lived Juno II launch vehicle, and sustaining a dedicated technical staff solely for a handful of Mercury capsule launches would have been cost-prohibitive.[[131]](#cite_note-141)

Orbital missions required use of the [Atlas LV-3B](/wiki/Atlas_LV-3B), a man-rated version of the [Atlas D](/wiki/SM-65D_Atlas) which was originally developed as the [United States](/wiki/United_States)' first operational [intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM)](/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile)[[132]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001211-142) by [Convair](/wiki/Convair) for the Air Force during the mid-1950s.[[133]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.196622-143) The Atlas was a "one-and-one-half-stage" rocket fueled by [kerosene](/wiki/Kerosene) and liquid [oxygen](/wiki/Oxygen) (LOX).[[132]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001211-142) The rocket by itself stood 67 feet (20 m) high; total height of the Atlas-Mercury space vehicle at launch was 95 feet (29 m).[[134]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001212-144)

The Atlas first stage was a booster skirt with two engines burning liquid fuel.[[135]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001225,_250-145)[[n 11]](#cite_note-146) This, together with the larger sustainer second stage, gave it sufficient power to launch a Mercury spacecraft into orbit.[[132]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001211-142) Both stages fired from lift-off with the thrust from the second stage sustainer engine passing through an opening in the first stage. After separation from the first stage, the sustainer stage continued alone. The sustainer also steered the rocket by thrusters guided by gyroscopes.[[136]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001458–459-147) Smaller vernier rockets were added on its sides for precise control of maneuvers.[[132]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001211-142)

/wiki/File:Project_Mercury-Mercury_Seven-Astronauts.jpgLeft to right: [Grissom](/wiki/Gus_Grissom), [Shepard](/wiki/Alan_Shepard), [Carpenter](/wiki/Scott_Carpenter), [Schirra](/wiki/Wally_Schirra), [Slayton](/wiki/Deke_Slayton), [Glenn](/wiki/John_Glenn) and [Cooper](/wiki/Gordon_Cooper), 1962
Alan Shepard became the first American in space by making a suborbital flight on May 5, 1961.[[139]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966341-150) [Mercury-Redstone 3](/wiki/Mercury-Redstone_3), Shepard's 15 minute and 28 second flight of the Freedom 7 capsule demonstrated the ability to withstand the high [g-forces](/wiki/G-force) of launch and [atmospheric re-entry](/wiki/Atmospheric_entry). Shepard later went on to fly in the [Apollo program](/wiki/Apollo_program) and became the only Mercury astronaut to walk on the Moon on [Apollo 14](/wiki/Apollo_14).[[140]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001445-151)[[141]](#cite_note-152)

[Gus Grissom](/wiki/Gus_Grissom) became the second American in space on [Mercury-Redstone 4](/wiki/Mercury-Redstone_4) on July 21, 1961. After the splashdown of Liberty Bell 7, the side hatch opened and caused the capsule to sink although Grissom was able to be safely recovered. His flight also gave NASA the confidence to move on to orbital flights. Grissom went on to participate in the Gemini and Apollo programs, but died in January 1967 during a pre-launch test for [Apollo 1](/wiki/Apollo_1).[[142]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001442-153)[[143]](#cite_note-154)

John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth on [Mercury-Atlas 6](/wiki/Mercury-Atlas_6) February 20, 1962. During the flight, the spacecraft Friendship 7 experienced issues with its automatic control system but Glenn was able to manually control the spacecraft's attitude. He quit NASA in 1964, when he came to the conclusion that he likely would not be selected for any Apollo missions, and was later elected to the US Senate, serving from 1974 to 1999. During his tenure, he returned to space in 1998 as a Payload Specialist aboard [STS-95](/wiki/STS-95).[[144]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001440,_441-155)[[145]](#cite_note-156)

Scott Carpenter was the second astronaut in orbit and flew on [Mercury-Atlas 7](/wiki/Mercury-Atlas_7) on May 24, 1962. The spaceflight was essentially a repeat of Mercury-Atlas 6, but a targeting error during re-entry took Aurora 7 250 miles (400 km) off-course, delaying recovery. Afterwards, he joined the Navy's "Man in the Sea" program and is the only American to be both an [astronaut](/wiki/Astronaut) and an [aquanaut](/wiki/Aquanaut).[[146]](#cite_note-157)[[147]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001446–447-158) Carpenter's Mercury flight was his only trip into space.

Wally Schirra flew aboard Sigma 7 on [Mercury-Atlas 8](/wiki/Mercury-Atlas_8) on October 3, 1962. The mission's main goal was to show development of environmental controls or life-support systems that would allow for safety in space, thus being a flight mainly focused on technical evaluation, rather than scientific experimentation. The mission lasted 9 hours and 13 minutes, setting a new US flight duration record.[[148]](#cite_note-159) In December 1965, Schirra flew on [Gemini 6A](/wiki/Gemini_6A), achieving the first ever [space rendezvous](/wiki/Space_rendezvous) with sister spacecraft [Gemini 7](/wiki/Gemini_7). Three years later, he commanded the first crewed Apollo mission, [Apollo 7](/wiki/Apollo_7), becoming the first astronaut to fly three times and the only person to fly in the Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo programs.

Gordon Cooper made the last flight of Project Mercury with [Mercury-Atlas 9](/wiki/Mercury-Atlas_9) on May 15, 1963. His flight onboard Faith 7 set another US endurance record with a 34-hour and 19 minute flight duration, and 22 completed orbits. This mission marks the last time an American was launched alone to conduct an entirely solo orbital mission. Cooper later went on to participate in [Project Gemini](/wiki/Project_Gemini) where he once again beat the endurance record during [Gemini 5](/wiki/Gemini_5).[[149]](#cite_note-160)[[150]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966640–641-161)

Deke Slayton was grounded in 1962 due to a heart condition, but remained with NASA and was appointed senior manager of the Astronaut Office and later additionally assistant director of Flight Crew Operations at the beginning of [Project Gemini](/wiki/Project_Gemini). On March 13, 1972, after doctors confirmed he no longer had a coronary condition, Slayton returned to flight status and the next year was assigned to the [Apollo–Soyuz Test Project](/wiki/Apollo%E2%80%93Soyuz_Test_Project), which successfully flew in 1975 with Slayton as the docking module pilot. After the ASTP, he managed the Space Shuttle Program's [Approach and Landing Tests](/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests) (ALT) and Orbital Flight Tests (OFT) before retiring from NASA in 1982.

One of the astronauts' tasks was publicity; they gave interviews to the press and visited project manufacturing facilities to speak with those who worked on Project Mercury.[[151]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200199-162) The press was especially fond of John Glenn, who was considered the best speaker of the seven.[[152]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200196-163) They sold their personal stories to [Life](/wiki/Life_(magazine)) magazine which portrayed them as 'patriotic, God-fearing family men.'[[153]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001100-164) Life was also allowed to be at home with the families while the astronauts were in space.[[153]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001100-164) During the project, Grissom, Carpenter, Cooper, Schirra and Slayton stayed with their families at or near Langley Air Force Base; Glenn lived at the base and visited his family in Washington DC on weekends. Shepard lived with his family at [Naval Air Station Oceana](/wiki/Naval_Air_Station_Oceana) in Virginia.

Other than Grissom, who was killed in the 1967 [Apollo 1](/wiki/Apollo_1) fire, the other six survived past retirement and died between 1993 and 2016.[[154]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200197-165)

### Selection and training
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Project_Mercury&action=edit&section=14)]

Prior to Project Mercury, there was no protocol for selecting astronauts, so NASA would set a far-reaching precedent with both their selection process and initial choices for astronauts. At the end of 1958, various ideas for the selection pool were discussed privately within the national government and the civilian space program, and also among the public at large. Initially, there was the idea to issue a widespread public call to volunteers. Thrill-seekers such as rock climbers and acrobats would have been allowed to apply, but this idea was quickly shot down by NASA officials who understood that an undertaking such as space flight required individuals with professional training and education in flight engineering. By late 1958, NASA officials decided to move forward with test pilots being the heart of their selection pool.[[156]](#cite_note-NASA-167) On President Eisenhower's insistence, the group was further narrowed down to active duty military [test pilots](/wiki/Test_pilot), which set the number of candidates at 508.[[157]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander_&_al.1966160–161-168) These candidates were [USN](/wiki/USN) or [USMC](/wiki/USMC) [naval aviation pilots](/wiki/United_States_Naval_Aviator) (NAPs), or [USAF](/wiki/USAF) [pilots of Senior or Command rating](/wiki/U.S._Air_Force_aeronautical_rating#USAF_rating_requirements). These aviators had long military records, which would give NASA officials more background information on which to base their decisions. Furthermore, these aviators were skilled in flying the most advanced aircraft to date, giving them the best qualifications for the new position of astronaut.[[156]](#cite_note-NASA-167) During this time, women were banned from flying in the military and so could not successfully qualify as test pilots. This meant that no female candidates could earn consideration for the title of astronaut. Civilian NASA [X-15](/wiki/X-15) pilot [Neil Armstrong](/wiki/Neil_Armstrong) was also disqualified, though he had been selected by the US Air Force in 1958 for its [Man in Space Soonest](/wiki/Man_in_Space_Soonest) program, which was replaced by Mercury.[[158]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansen2005173-169) Although Armstrong had been a combat-experienced NAP during the Korean War, he left active duty in 1952.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200192-8)[[n 12]](#cite_note-171) Armstrong became NASA's first civilian astronaut in 1962 when he was selected for NASA's second group,[[160]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansen2005201–202-172) and [became the first man on the Moon](/wiki/Apollo_11) in 1969.[[161]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson200917-173)

It was further stipulated that candidates should be between 25 and 40 years old, no taller than 5 ft 11 in (1.80 m), and hold a college degree in a [STEM](/wiki/Science,_technology,_engineering,_and_mathematics) subject.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200192-8) The college degree requirement excluded the USAF's [X-1](/wiki/Bell_X-1) pilot, then-Lt Col (later Brig Gen) [Chuck Yeager](/wiki/Chuck_Yeager), the first person to exceed the [speed of sound](/wiki/Speed_of_sound).[[162]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200192–93-174) He later became a critic of the project, ridiculing the civilian space program, labeling astronauts as "spam in a can."[[163]](#cite_note-175) John Glenn did not have a college degree either, but used influential friends to make the selection committee accept him.[[164]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2001440-176) USAF Capt. (later Col.) [Joseph Kittinger](/wiki/Joseph_Kittinger), a USAF fighter pilot and stratosphere balloonist, met all the requirements but preferred to stay in his contemporary project.[[162]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200192–93-174) Other potential candidates declined because they did not believe that human spaceflight had a future beyond Project Mercury.[[162]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200192–93-174)[[n 13]](#cite_note-178) From the original 508, 110 candidates were selected for an interview, and from the interviews, 32 were selected for further physical and mental testing.[[166]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200193-179) Their health, vision, and hearing were examined, together with their tolerance to noise, vibrations, g-forces, personal isolation, and heat.[[167]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200198-180)[[168]](#cite_note-181) In a special chamber, they were tested to see if they could perform their tasks under confusing conditions.[[167]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200198-180) The candidates had to answer more than 500 questions about themselves and describe what they saw in different images.[[167]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200198-180) Navy Lt (later Capt) [Jim Lovell](/wiki/Jim_Lovell), who was later an astronaut in the [Gemini](/wiki/Project_Gemini) and [Apollo programs](/wiki/Apollo_program), did not pass the physical tests.[[162]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200192–93-174) After these tests it was intended to narrow the group down to six astronauts, but in the end it was decided to keep seven.[[169]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole200194
